Science · Nobel Chemistry Prize · The Big Story

The molecule made more of itself. Then it changed chemistry.

Kenso Soai’s experiment begins with molecules that appear equivalent, like left and right hands. One side gains the slightest lead. What happens next is the discovery Stockholm honored—and a clue to why life itself chose a side.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 8, 2026 · 9 min read

Kenso Soai was not standing beneath laboratory lights when the call came. According to the Associated Press, the 76-year-old chemist was shopping at a neighborhood supermarket when he learned that he and French chemist Henri B. Kagan, 95, had won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. An ordinary errand had been interrupted by a message about one of chemistry’s most extraordinary imbalances.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the pair the prize “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.” The language is dense; the central image is not. Hold out your hands. They have the same parts arranged in mirror-image forms, yet one hand cannot be rotated to fit perfectly over the other. Many molecules have this same property. Chemists call it chirality, from the Greek word for hand.

That difference can matter enormously. Two mirror forms can behave differently inside a biological system because the receptors, enzymes and proteins they meet are themselves three-dimensional. A molecule’s “right” and “left” versions may share a formula while interacting differently with the body. Making the desired version cleanly is therefore not an aesthetic problem. It is central to modern pharmaceutical and materials chemistry.

The mystery hiding in the mirror

Nature presents a deeper puzzle. Laboratory synthesis can produce both mirror forms in equal amounts. Living systems, however, overwhelmingly use one handedness for major building blocks: amino acids in proteins are predominantly left-handed, while the sugars in DNA and RNA have the opposite convention. This homochirality is essential to life as we know it, but how a world with no initial preference could produce such a powerful preference has troubled chemists for more than a century.

Kagan supplied one part of the answer. His work on non-linear effects showed that a small imbalance in a chiral catalyst did not always yield a proportionally small imbalance in the product. Chemistry could magnify the preference. The output did not have to track the input in a neat, straight line.

Soai pursued a stranger possibility. While studying asymmetric reactions, he noticed a structural resemblance between a catalyst and the substance a reaction produced. Could the product itself become the catalyst for making more product? And if that product had a handedness, could it preferentially reproduce that same handedness?

The answer was yes—and that is the avalanche promised by the headline. In the Soai reaction, the chiral product acts as a catalyst for its own formation. A minute initial excess of one mirror form can be amplified through repeated cycles into an overwhelmingly one-sided result.

A product that recruits its own copies

Soai’s group reported its landmark asymmetric autocatalysis in 1995 using a pyrimidyl alcohol formed by adding diisopropylzinc to a pyrimidine aldehyde. The names are less important than the feedback loop. The product helps create more product. Crucially, a product of one handedness helps create more molecules of the same handedness.

The Royal Society of Chemistry’s overview describes an early demonstration in which material beginning with only 2% enantiomeric excess reached 88% after consecutive autocatalytic cycles. The tiny lead did not remain tiny. Each round strengthened it. Later versions achieved still more dramatic amplification from extremely small starting imbalances.

self-copying feedback →
After cyclesmostly leftvery little right

This is not proof that the Soai reaction itself began life on Earth. Its laboratory reagents are not a reconstruction of a primordial ocean. The scientific significance is more careful and, in a way, more powerful: the reaction demonstrates a chemically plausible mechanism by which a nearly imperceptible asymmetry can become dominant. It turns a philosophical “how could one side win?” into an experimentally testable process.

Why the Nobel committee paired two chemists

The award links Kagan’s non-linear effects with Soai’s asymmetric autocatalysis because they explain complementary stages of symmetry breaking. Kagan showed that the relationship between a catalyst’s handedness and its product could bend away from simple proportionality. Soai created a reaction in which the favored product helps reproduce and amplify itself.

Science Portal, operated by the Japan Science and Technology Agency, reports that the Nobel committee described the Soai reaction as one of chemistry’s most astonishing experiments. It credits the laureates with providing a solution to the question of how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The word “solution” here describes a mechanism, not the final historical account of how terrestrial life began.

The prize also carries a generational story. Kagan was born in 1931 and is now 95. Soai was born in Hiroshima in 1950, earned his doctorate at the University of Tokyo, worked as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of North Carolina, and built his career at Tokyo University of Science. The university notes that he received Japan’s Medal with Purple Ribbon in 2012. In 2025, the Japan Academy honored the Soai reaction for advancing the study of the origin of homochirality.

A second consecutive chemistry celebration for Japan

Soai is Japan’s tenth chemistry laureate, according to Science Portal, and his award follows Susumu Kitagawa’s share of the 2025 chemistry prize for metal–organic frameworks. That sequence is remarkable, but it should not collapse two very different accomplishments into a national scoreboard. Kitagawa’s porous structures created new spaces for chemistry; Soai’s work asks how chemical identity can select and reinforce itself.

The 2026 prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, to be divided equally between Soai and Kagan. The award ceremony is scheduled for December 10 in Stockholm, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death. Those are the formal markers. The more durable measure will be how researchers use the concepts of feedback, amplification and symmetry breaking to design new reactions—and to sharpen questions about the chemical boundary between nonlife and life.

What the discovery does—and does not—mean for medicine

Asymmetric chemistry underpins the production of many medicines, and experts interviewed by AP emphasized that modern drug development depends on the ability to choose molecular handedness. But it would be misleading to say that every chiral medicine is manufactured with the Soai reaction. The reaction’s direct industrial use is narrower than the broad importance of the principles it revealed.

Its greatest influence is conceptual. Chemists learned that autocatalysis, selectivity and a non-linear response can work together. That framework helps researchers think about new self-amplifying systems, methods for detecting tiny chiral influences, and models of spontaneous symmetry breaking. The chemistry prize recognizes a foundation from which other tools can grow.

The ordinary scene after the extraordinary call

There is something fitting about the supermarket story. A store is full of chemical handedness that no shopper needs to see: sugars, amino acids, aromas and medicines all depend on three-dimensional fit. The shelves look symmetrical enough. At molecular scale, life is not.

Soai told the Nobel committee that receiving the news was among the most exciting moments of his life. The statement is personal; the experiment is universal. Begin with two mirror possibilities. Add the faintest preference. Let the winner help make more of itself. The decimal becomes a direction, and the direction becomes a world.

Today’s Japanese word, 鏡像 (kyōzō), means “mirror image.” It is a useful word for the discovery and a useful reminder: two things can look identical in every ordinary description and still behave as fundamentally different shapes.
